extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public relations and government/military public affairs
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter describing roles, duties, principles, challenges, and professional standards for government and military public affairs officers, including DoD 'Principles of Information' and practices such as embedding journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary roles of military public affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide information to the public about military policies and operations; enhance morale of service members; and showcase the efforts and accomplishments of service members so that an informed citizenry and their elected representatives have the best information available when making decisions about military policy and operations. Military public affairs has no role in advancing or supporting a political agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes military PA from political communications (e.g., Pentagon news conferences by political appointees may aim to garner public support). Emphasizes informing rather than influencing public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core duties of military public affairs officers (PAOs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct planned and sustained programs on behalf of military leadership; manage relationships between the military organization and its publics; monitor awareness, opinions, attitudes, and behavior inside and outside the organization; advise leadership on adjustments when policies conflict with public interest or military effectiveness; counsel on establishing policies mutually beneficial to military and publics; establish and maintain two-way communication; produce specific changes in awareness, opinions, attitudes, and behaviors inside the military and externally; and create or maintain relationships between the military and its publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These duties frame PAOs as strategic counselors and relationship managers rather than mere information clerks. Organizationally similar to corporate public relations but with unique internal-relations responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal information program responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal relations (employee communication) are the domain of military public affairs because all service members are de facto spokespersons for their services and must understand the service and their command's mission and vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why internal communications reside in PA rather than HR in the military: many HR policies and benefits are decided by Congress, creating a public as well as internal information need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: Make information fully and readily available (DoD)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information shall be made fully and readily available, consistent with statutory requirements, unless its release is precluded by national security constraints or valid statutory mandates or exceptions. The Freedom of Information Act will be supported in both letter and spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames availability as default; exceptions must be grounded in law or security. Ties to FOIA and open-government statutes mentioned earlier in chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: Free flow of information without censorship or propaganda (DoD)
rubrics_metrics.description: A free flow of general and military information shall be made available, without censorship or propaganda, to the men and women of the Armed Forces and their dependents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly rejects propaganda in PA programs and underscores uncensored informational flow to internal and external publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: Do not withhold information to avoid criticism or embarrassment (DoD)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information will not be classified or otherwise withheld to protect the Government from criticism or embarrassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Places ethical constraint on classification/withholding that is motivated by bureaucratic self-protection rather than legitimate security or legal reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: Withhold information when disclosure would harm security, privacy, or violate law (DoD)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information shall be withheld when disclosure would adversely affect national security, threaten the safety or privacy of U.S. Government personnel or their families, violate the privacy of U.S. citizens, or be contrary to law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies legitimate, concrete reasons to limit disclosure and frames them as acceptable exceptions to the default of availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle: Detailed PA planning and coordination for major programs; no propaganda (DoD)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department of Defense’s obligation to provide the public with information on DoD major programs may require detailed Public Affairs planning and coordination in the Department of Defense and with other Government Agencies; such activity is to expedite information flow to the public; propaganda has no place in DoD public affairs programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stresses the need for deliberate planning and interagency coordination for major program communications while reiterating the prohibition on propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embed journalists as a transparency strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Embedding journalists with military units (e.g., during Operation Iraqi Freedom) can provide unprecedented access, humanize both journalists and soldiers, improve understanding of military life, serve as a link back to home audiences, increase trust, and improve military–media relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides practical example (USS Constellation embed) and notes operational challenges (language/cultural differences, logistical/discipline issues, 24-hour news demands) as well as benefits such as better information exchange and empathetic coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance transparency with operational security
rubrics_metrics.description: Communications must weigh the need to inform the public against the requirement to protect operational security; disclosing certain information can endanger soldiers on the battlefield.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges a core tension unique to military PA: transparency and engagement are important, but some details must be withheld to protect lives and missions. PAOs must be sophisticated and strategic in managing that balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of access for media to government information (FOIA & sunshine laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Except for well-defined areas (national security, litigation, certain personnel records, etc.), virtually every piece of government information is open to inspection by the press and public; reporters can demand unfinished drafts and notes if they have specific knowledge and request them with adequate specificity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positions media access as legally and democratically important—supports watchdog role, accountability, and crystallizing public issues—while recognizing valid carve-outs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work with journalists given differing standards of newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters and government communicators use different standards to define news; much important agency information can be lost amid competing news priorities and limited newsroom resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why PAOs are essential in helping journalists interpret complex government topics (e.g., international trade, nuclear issues, mental health) and why sustained relationships and explanations are necessary to get coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalization and training of military public affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Military public affairs has been professionalized through formal training (Defense Information School), university programs (e.g., SDSU accelerated master's for active-duty PAOs), and accreditation (PRSA APR), improving strategic thinking and theory-based practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides an example of a DoD–university program and participant testimony that formal education enhances strategic capacity and daily performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barriers limiting effectiveness of government public affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Three major barriers limit effectiveness: public apathy (lack of interest among citizens), legislative hostility (congressional restrictions and suspicion, e.g., the 1913 Gillett Amendment), and adversarial government–media relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives historical examples (Pinchot and Forest Service publicity, congressional reactions, Gillett Amendment) and explains how these barriers complicate outreach, constrain resources, and foster confusion or concealment practices.
